(CNN) — Michael Vick, the former quarterback for the Atlanta Falcons, returned Thursday morning to his residence in Hampton, Virginia.

Vick, a Newport News, Virginia, native, was released Wednesday from a federal prison in Leavenworth, Kansas. According to his publicist, Judy Smith, he will spend the final two months of his 23-month sentence under home confinement in Virginia.

Chris Garrett, a spokesman for Vick, said the former NFL player was pleased to be back with his family.

In August 2007, Vick, then 28, admitted guilt to a federal charge related to financing a dogfighting operation at a Virginia property he owned. If the NFL reinstates him, he could potentially resume his professional football career as early as September, according to the sports agent who helped negotiate Vick’s 10-year, $140 million deal with the Falcons.

Vick’s lawyers have also said that, following his release, he plans to take a job with a construction company in Newport News. In addition, he has agreed to take part in a documentary for $600,000.

The month before his release, U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Frank Santoro rejected a Chapter 11 bankruptcy proposal submitted by Vick and encouraged him to file a revised plan. Santoro said the rejected proposal required Vick to provide between $750,000 and $1 million in cash for creditors, but the judge said he had not seen proof that Vick could raise that amount. Santoro also recommended that any new proposal not include Vick keeping two homes and three vehicles, as the rejected version had.

During testimony, Vick described his conduct as “heinous” and said he should have behaved with greater maturity. He also said he had been working in prison as an overnight janitor for 12 cents an hour. By contrast, he said his salary with the Falcons had been between $10 million and $12 million. Vick acknowledged that he had mismanaged his finances.

Wayne Pacelle, president of the Humane Society of the United States, told CNN on Tuesday that after Vick’s release, he would partner with the organization on campaigns opposing dogfighting. Pacelle said Vick would be involved in efforts designed both to keep young people from entering dogfighting and to help youths who had already participated in the activity.

Pacelle said Vick’s representatives had contacted the Humane Society. He said he visited Kansas twice to meet with the former quarterback. During their second meeting, Pacelle said, they talked about how Vick could use his influence with young people to steer them away from dogfighting and assist those who had been caught up in it. The specific arrangements had not yet been finalized, Pacelle said, but were expected to be completed within a few days.

Pacelle also said Vick’s case had brought increased public focus to dogfighting. The Humane Society, which pays rewards for information related to dogfighting, had recently distributed $40,000 in five cases, he said.

CNN’s Marylynn Ryan contributed to the report.
